title.text: Forecasting and a first end-to-end model: baseline, time-based split and Pipeline

objects.text: How do we predict next month, and how do we pack a whole modelling job into one object we can trust?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 19 of 24  |  Module D: Machine learning
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. For five sessions you have built models that predict a label or a number from a table. Today the table has a calendar in it, and one rule changes completely: the future is hidden, and a fair test must hide it too. We forecast malaria cases for twelve districts, we meet the baseline that every model must beat, and we pack the whole job into one object called a Pipeline.

Today is Project milestone 3, and the result you build goes into your course project.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can split a time series by date, and you can explain why a random split lets the model peek at the future. You can beat a seasonal naive baseline using lag features, and report the error in cases with three measures: MAE, RMSE and MAPE.

And you can pack the whole job into a scikit-learn Pipeline and write your Project milestone 3 result in three sentences. We use the District Clinics file, twelve districts and five years of malaria cases.

title.text:
Your two hours: forecasting ideas
first, then the Project milestone 3 lab

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x2.95_e01d7d89.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Ideas with pictures first. Then you open the notebook, forecast 2025 and write your result.

slides.notes:
We have two hours, and today produces Project milestone 3. The first ten minutes bring back Session 18 and set the question. Then forty-five minutes of concepts with laptops closed: what a time series is, the baseline you must beat, the split by date, lag features, the three error measures, and the Pipeline.

After a ten minute break you open the notebook for a forty-five minute lab. You forecast 2025 for twelve districts and write your result. The last ten minutes are the exit check and what you keep.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What is learning without a target variable called, and how did we judge the customer segments?
2.  Why did we standardise the variables before running k-means?
3.  What does the elbow method plot, and what do you look for?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 18. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What is learning without a target variable called, and how did we judge the customer segments?

A good answer is this. Unsupervised learning. With no right answer to check, we judged each cluster by whether it could be described in business words and acted on.

Question two. Why did we standardise the variables before running k-means?

A good answer is this. k-means works with distances. A variable in large units, such as spend in UGX, would swamp a variable in small units, such as visits.

Question three. What does the elbow method plot, and what do you look for?

A good answer is this. The inertia (within-cluster sum of squares) for each k. You look for the bend where another cluster stops reducing it much.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

Here are the answers to the three warm-up questions. Learning without a target variable is unsupervised learning. Because there was no right answer to check against, we judged each cluster by whether we could describe it in business words and act on it. And the elbow method plots the inertia for each k, and we look for the bend. Today the answers come back in a new form: we will predict a number that we can check against what really happened. Which of the three did you find hardest?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: One variable recorded at regular times, such as cases each month. It splits into a slow trend, a yearly seasonality and leftover noise.
The simplest forecast: copy the same month from last year. A model must beat it to be worth using.
Train on the months before a cut date and test on the months after it. Never split a time series at random.
An earlier value placed in the same row, such as last month's cases. It is built inside each district.
Preprocessing steps and a model packed into one object, so training and test records go through the same steps.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Time series (trend, seasonality, noise). One variable recorded at regular times, such as cases each month. It splits into a slow trend, a yearly seasonality and leftover noise.

Baseline model (seasonal naive forecast). The simplest forecast: copy the same month from last year. A model must beat it to be worth using.

Time-based split (temporal split). Train on the months before a cut date and test on the months after it. Never split a time series at random.

Lag feature. An earlier value placed in the same row, such as last month's cases. It is built inside each district.

Pipeline (scikit-learn). Preprocessing steps and a model packed into one object, so training and test records go through the same steps.

title.text:
A time series is one variable recorded at
regular times: here 60 months for 12 districts

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_sheet_7.70x4.80_f844e2ff.png
objects.alt: A time series is one variable recorded at regular times: here 60 months for 12 districts

objects.text: A time series is a variable recorded at regular times, in time order.

runs.text: Each record is one district in one month: 720 records from clinic_visits.csv.
The picture shows the first months of Gulu, from 2021-01.
Forecasting means predicting the next values of the series.

slides.notes:
Our data for today is the District Clinics file. Each record is one district in one month, and there are 12 districts and 60 months, January 2021 to December 2025, so 720 records. The picture shows the first four months of Gulu. The variable we want to predict is malaria cases, the gold cell.

A variable recorded at regular times and kept in time order is called a time series. In Excel it is a column of monthly figures with the dates beside it. Forecasting means predicting the next values of that column. What would you want to forecast in your own work?

title.text:
A time series splits into trend,
seasonality and noise (decomposition)

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsj_decomp_11.90x4.25_71d0c766.png
objects.alt: A time series splits into trend, seasonality and noise (decomposition)

objects.text: All 12 districts added up. Trend: about 69 more cases a month. Noise: the rest.

slides.notes:
Here is the total of all twelve districts, pulled apart into three pieces. This is called a decomposition. The trend is the slow drift. I fitted a straight line to it, and it rises by about 69 cases each month. The seasonality is the shape that repeats every year, and it moves the total by about 5,582 cases from its lowest month to its highest.

The noise is what is left over, and no model can predict it. A forecast can use the trend and the seasonality. It can never use the noise. Which of the three would a manager find most useful?

title.text:
Seasonality repeats every year: December
is the peak and September is the trough

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsj_columns_11.90x4.25_c017da95.png
objects.alt: Seasonality repeats every year: December is the peak and September is the trough

objects.text: Cases of all 12 districts over five years, added for each calendar month. Gold: the peak.

slides.notes:
This picture adds every January of the five years into one column, every February into the next, and so on. December is the tallest at 152,876 cases, the gold column. September is the lowest at 123,931. The columns are far from equal: April to June and October to December are higher than the months around them.

That repeating shape is seasonality, and it is what makes forecasting possible. If every month looked the same, last month would tell us everything. Because the year has a shape, the same month a year ago is already a decent guess. What seasonal pattern do you see in your own work?

title.text: The forecast horizon is how far ahead you predict

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsj_horizon_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The forecast horizon is how far ahead you predict

objects.text: Horizon: months between the last month you know and the month you predict. Today: horizon 1.

slides.notes:
Every forecast has a forecast horizon, the number of months between the last month you know and the month you want to predict. The black squares are the months you know. The red line is today. Horizon 1 means next month. Horizon 3 means three months ahead, and horizon 12 means a whole year ahead.

The horizon matters because a forecast gets harder the further ahead you look, and later we measure by how much. Today we forecast with horizon 1, and the lab makes you say so in your report. What horizon would a pharmacy stock planner need?

title.text:
The baseline model is a seasonal naive
forecast: copy the same month from last year

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsj_lines_11.90x4.25_70475fbe.png
objects.alt: The baseline model is a seasonal naive forecast: copy the same month from last year

objects.text: Forecast for January 2025 = January 2024. Mbarara 2025: average miss 623 cases.

slides.notes:
Before any clever model, we build the baseline model, the simplest forecast that could work. The seasonal naive forecast copies the same month from last year. So January 2025 is predicted by January 2024. In Excel it is a formula that points twelve rows up. The picture shows Mbarara.

The black line is what happened, and the dashed red line is the copy of the year before. It follows the shape, but it misses the peaks. The average miss for Mbarara in 2025 is 623 cases a month. Every model we build today must beat this baseline, or it is not worth using.

title.text:
Mean absolute error (MAE) is the
average size of the errors, in cases

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.96_3839bc6f.png
objects.alt: Mean absolute error (MAE) is the average size of the errors, in cases

rows.text: The actual value for month i.

objects.text: MAE is in the unit of the target: cases. The sum of the 12 absolute errors is 7,479.

slides.notes:
Now we need a number for how wrong a forecast is. The mean absolute error, MAE, takes each miss, which is actual minus forecast, drops the sign, and averages. The symbol y is the actual value and y-hat is the forecast. The bars mean absolute value, so a miss of plus five hundred and a miss of minus five hundred both count as five hundred.

For Mbarara the twelve absolute misses add up to 7,479. Divide by twelve and the MAE is 623.25 cases. The great advantage is the unit. A manager hears cases and understands. Why would we drop the sign before averaging?

title.text:
MAE, RMSE and MAPE are three
ways to score the same forecast

rows.text: Square each miss, average, take the square root. Big misses count more.
Average of |miss| divided by actual, times 100

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_coin_0.50.png

objects.text: Scores on the 144 district-months of 2025. MAPE cannot be used when an actual value can be 0.

slides.notes:
Three scores for one forecast. MAE is the average miss in cases. RMSE squares each miss, averages, and takes the square root, so one large miss hurts it far more than many small ones. MAPE divides each miss by the actual value, so it gives a percentage, and it fails when an actual value can be zero.

On the 2025 test the baseline scores 460.7 on MAE, 748.6 on RMSE and 18.5 percent on MAPE. The lag model, which we build in a moment, scores 338.0, 490.9 and 16.3. Which would you report to a manager, and which to a data team?

title.text:
A time-based split trains on the
past and tests on the future

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsj_timesplit_11.90x4.25_1a38ea99.png
objects.alt: A time-based split trains on the past and tests on the future

objects.text: Next month always lies after everything you know, so the test must too.

slides.notes:
In Session 14 you split the loans at random. A time series changes the rule. The split must follow the calendar. In the top strip the test months, in gold, are scattered, so some training months come after the test months. The model has seen the future. In the bottom strip we cut at the first of January 2025.

We train on the earlier months and test on the 144 records of 2025. That is a time-based split, also called a temporal split. It copies real life, because next month always lies after everything you know. Why does a scattered test set look unfair to you?

title.text: Data leakage from the future flatters a score

objects.text: Looks ahead (leaks)

runs.text: A random split moved MAE only a little here (332.2 against 338.0), but trend raises the risk.
A shift(-1) feature holds next month: MAE falls from 304.8 to 265.5.

objects.text: Safe

runs.text: Cut at a date: train before, test after.
Use the past only: shift(1) or more.

objects.text: A feature absent on forecast day must go.

slides.notes:
Data leakage means information from outside the training period slips into the model. Two forms matter for a time series. A random split puts later months in the training set. And a feature built with shift minus one holds next month, which you will never know on the day you forecast.

Look at the number. On one random split, adding that next-month feature cuts the MAE from 304.8 to 265.5. That looks like progress, but it is borrowed from the future. Notice also that our simple linear model scores 332.2 on a random split and 338.0 on the date split, almost the same.

Nothing warns you, which is why we follow the rule. These numbers come from one seeded split and are not in the lab. Which feature in your own data might look ahead?

title.text:
Last month's rain relates to malaria cases
(r=0.37) but this month's rain does not (r=0.02)

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsj_scatter2_11.90x4.25_360c6bab.png
objects.alt: Last month's rain relates to malaria cases (r=0.37) but this month's rain does not (r=0.02)

objects.text: Each dot is one district-month (576 in all). r is the Pearson correlation.

slides.notes:
Why would we bring earlier values into a row?

Look at rain. On the left, each dot is one district in one month, 576 dots, with rainfall in the same month. The correlation is 0.02, almost nothing. On the right, the same cases against the rainfall of the month before. The correlation is 0.37, and the red line clearly climbs.

The effect of rain comes with a delay, and a plausible reason is that standing water needs time to produce mosquitoes. A model that sees only this month's rain would miss it. A model that is given last month's rain finds it. What delayed effect exists in your own work?

title.text:
A lag feature puts an earlier
value into the same row

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_sheet_7.70x4.80_e3b8a9dc.png
objects.alt: A lag feature puts an earlier value into the same row

objects.text: A lag feature is the value of a variable some months earlier, in the same record.

runs.text: cases_lag1 is last month. cases_lag12 is the same month last year.
Gulu, 2022-01: the lag 12 value 3794 is the cases of 2021-01.
The first rows have no lag, so they are blank.

slides.notes:
A lag feature is the value of a variable some months earlier, placed in the same record. In the picture, cases lag one is last month and cases lag twelve is the same month last year. Look at the gold cell. For Gulu in 2022-01, the lag twelve value is 3794, which is the cases of 2021-01, a year earlier.

In Excel you would type equals B2 one row down. In pandas it is the shift function. The first rows of each district have no earlier value, so they are blank. Why would we need to throw those rows away before fitting?

title.text:
A lag built without groupby borrows
values from the district above it

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_flagged_sheet_11.90x4.25_0bc1cdb9.png
objects.alt: A lag built without groupby borrows values from the district above it

objects.text: Without groupby: 11 wrong lag 1 and 132 wrong lag 12 values. Test MAE 366.3.

slides.notes:
This trap raises no error. The file is stacked, one district after another, sorted by district and month. If you shift the whole column, the first month of Gulu receives the last month of the district above it. Here that is 3074, the December 2025 cases of Fort Portal.

Across the file, 11 districts get a wrong lag one and 132 records get a wrong lag twelve. On our data the test MAE becomes 366.3 instead of 338.0. The cure is to group by district before you shift, and to check one first row by hand. Why does Python give no warning?

title.text:
Lag features cost records: 720 become
576, then 432 to train and 144 to test

rows.text: The first 12 months of each district have no lag 12: 144 lost

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_grid_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_calendar_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_flag_0.50.png

objects.text: Lost rows are an expected cost. A lag needs history.

slides.notes:
Lag features cost records. We start with 720, twelve districts times sixty months. A lag of twelve months needs a year of history, so the first twelve months of each district have no value, and 144 records drop out. That leaves 576. We cut at the first of January 2025.

The training set is twenty twenty-two to twenty twenty-four, 432 records, and the test set is the twelve months of 2025, 144 records. Dropping the early rows is a normal cost of the method. A lag simply needs history. Check these counts in the lab, because every later number depends on them.

How many records would you keep if the lag were 24 months?

title.text:
Read the recipe: lag features inside
each district, then a split at the cut date

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Line 1 sorts by district and month. Line 2 groups by district, so every shift stays inside one district.
Lines 3 to 5 build the three lag features.
Line 7 drops the records that have no lag.

slides.notes:
Read this recipe before the lab. Line one sorts the records by district and month, and line two groups them by district, so every shift stays inside one district. Lines three to five build the three lag features: last month's cases, the cases of the same month last year, and last month's rainfall.

Line seven drops the records that have no lag. Lines eight and nine cut the calendar at the first of January 2025. The last line prints four counts, and the output is real, from the clinic file. 720, then 576, then 432 and 144. These match the table you just saw.

Which line would you change for a lag of two months?

title.text:
Fit on the past, test on 2025:
the lag model beats the baseline

objects.text:
baseline 460.7
model    338.0
In plain words

runs.text: Lines 1 to 3 fit a linear regression with numpy, using only the training set.
The coefficients are the intercept and one weight for each lag feature.
y_pred holds the forecast for each test record.
The baseline misses by 460.7 cases on average. The model misses by 338.0.

slides.notes:
Now we fit. The first three lines fit a linear regression with numpy, using only the training set, and then predict the test set. The model is the intercept plus a weight for each lag feature. The last two lines score the baseline and the model on the 2025 test, as the average absolute miss in cases.

The baseline misses by 460.7 cases a month on average. The lag model misses by 338.0. That is 27 percent smaller. The printed numbers are real output from the clinic file. Does a smaller number alone tell you the model is good enough? I will answer that in a moment.

title.text:
Judge the error in cases: an average miss
of 338 is 14 percent of a typical month

objects.text: The lag model misses by 338.0 cases on average. The mean district-month in 2025 had 2,403 cases. The baseline misses by 19 percent of that.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_waffle_4.40x4.30_48d33acc.png
objects.alt: Judge the error in cases: an average miss of 338 is 14 percent of a typical month

slides.notes:
A score only matters in the unit of the decision. The lag model misses by 338.0 cases on average, and the mean district month in 2025 had 2,403 cases. So the average miss is about 14 percent of that. This differs from the MAPE of 16.3 percent, because MAPE averages the percentage miss of each month and small months weigh more.

The baseline misses by about 19 percent. A district manager can plan stock around that: keep enough medicine for about 338 more cases than you expect. One caution. It is an average, so some months and districts miss by much more, and we say that when we report.

How would you phrase this for a manager in one sentence?

title.text:
The model beats the baseline on
average but not in every district

An average hides differences. Here are six districts, with the typical monthly cases and the MAE of the baseline and of the model. In Gulu, Mbarara and Mukono the model is clearly better. In Jinja, Kabale and Kampala the baseline wins. Those are the districts with fewer cases, where the baseline already misses by little.

Over all twelve districts the model has the lower error in 9, and in 83 of the 144 district months. So the honest report says the model is better on average, and it names where it is not. Why might a simple copy work well for a small district?

objects.text: Each row refits the model with lags that are known h months ahead. Same train and test split.

slides.notes:
The forecast horizon changes the answer. For horizon one, we know last month, so the model uses it, and the MAE is 338.0. For horizon three, the most recent month we know is three months back, so the model has to use older lags, and the MAE rises to 448.3.

At six months it is 430.4, lower than at three months, so the loss of skill is not a straight line. At twelve months the model has only the year-old values, and the MAE is 480.1, which is worse than the baseline of 460.7. The lesson is to state the horizon with every forecast.

Which horizon does your own decision need?

title.text:
Walk-forward validation repeats the cut
date, so one lucky year cannot fool you

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_calendar_0.39.png

objects.text: Walk-forward validation (expanding window). In scikit-learn the same idea is TimeSeriesSplit.

slides.notes:
One test year is a single test. Walk-forward validation repeats it. We cut at the first of January 2023, train on the 144 records of 2022, and test on 2023. Then we move the cut to 2024, train on 288 records, and test on 2024. Then the cut for 2025, the one we used, trains on 432.

The model wins in all three years: 327.6, 336.8 and 338.0 against baselines of 484.6, 469.3 and 460.7. That makes the result far more believable than one year alone. Would you trust a model that won in only one of three years?

title.text:
A Pipeline packs preprocessing
and the model into one object

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsj_pipeline_11.90x4.25_fa99bae0.png
objects.alt: A Pipeline packs preprocessing and the model into one object

objects.text: One object to fit, one to predict, one to save. It also stops test records leaking into the preprocessing.

slides.notes:
So far we did each step by hand. That works, but it is easy to forget a step on the test data, or to run the steps in another order next month. A Pipeline fixes that. It is a list of steps that always run in the same order.

Here the steps are an imputer that fills blanks with the median, a scaler that standardises each variable, and the linear regression. When you call fit, each step learns only from the training records. When you call predict, the same steps run on the test records. In Excel it is a recorded macro you can run again on next month's file.

Which steps would your own pipeline need?

title.text:
Read the recipe: a scikit-learn Pipeline
gives the same forecast in a few lines

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: make_pipeline chains the three steps in order.
fit learns the median, the mean and the weights from the training records only.
predict runs the same steps on the test records.
The MAE is 338.0, the same as the numpy fit: standardising does not change a linear regression forecast.

slides.notes:
Here is the recipe. Make pipeline chains the three steps in order. The fit line learns the median, the mean and the weights from the training records only. The predict line runs the same steps on the test records. The printed MAE is 338.0, exactly the number we got with numpy.

That is a useful check: scaling the variables does not change what a linear regression forecasts, so the two methods must agree, and they do. The real work of a Pipeline shows when you add steps, as you will see shortly. Why is it good news that two different methods agree?

title.text:
Adding the district as indicator variables
lowers the MAE from 338 to 217

rows.text: Same Pipeline with 11 district indicator variables

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_gear_0.39.png

objects.text: One-hot encoding: district becomes 0/1 indicator (dummy) variables. Drop one district to avoid the dummy variable trap. In scikit-learn: ColumnTransformer and OneHotEncoder.

slides.notes:
Districts differ a lot in size. Kampala has about 648 cases in a typical month and Mukono about 4,250. If the model also knows which district it is forecasting, it can correct for that. We add the district as indicator variables, columns of zero and one, which is called one-hot encoding.

Eleven columns plus the three lags make 14 variables, and the MAE falls from 338.0 to 217.1. In scikit-learn the encoding goes inside the Pipeline with a ColumnTransformer and a OneHotEncoder. In the lab we create the columns with pandas, which gives the same forecast. Which variable would you add for your own district?

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: The cut date or the dropna step differs.
Use month >= '2025-01-01' and drop records missing a lag first.
The model scores worse than the baseline
The features or the lag direction are wrong.
Check that you used shift(1). A shift(-1) looks ahead. Check the sort order.
A lag feature is blank in a test record.
Drop the blank records with dropna(subset=features) before you split.
The lag column was not created, or it has another name.
Run the lag cell again, and check the spelling.
Your MAE differs from the table by a little
A different cut date, features or dropped row.
Below 0.1 case is rounding. Larger means other features.

Five messages you may meet. A test set that is not 144 records means the cut date or the dropna step is different, so cut at the first of January 2025 and drop the records with a missing lag first. If the model is worse than the baseline, check that you used shift one, because shift minus one looks ahead, and that the table is sorted.

NaN in the predictions means a blank lag feature reached the test set. A KeyError means the lag column was never created. And a tiny difference in the MAE is fine. Read the message first. It usually tells you the answer.

title.text:
Exit check: three questions, then
compare with the short answers

rows.text: A seasonal naive forecast for March 2026 uses which number?
The March 2025 value: the same month last year.
Why must a forecast be tested on later months?
Next month always lies after the data you have. A random split lets the model see the future, which is data leakage.
Your model misses by 338 cases and the baseline by 461. What do you tell the manager?
It beats the baseline by about 27 percent, with an average miss near 338 cases at horizon 1, but some districts and months miss by more.
